headline: Curaleaf clears German and Canadian antitrust reviews for Aurora bid
dek: Curaleaf said on 10 November its hostile offer for Aurora Cannabis needs no more competition approvals, raising pressure on Organigram's agreed C$7.80 deal.
key_points: Curaleaf said on 10 November that Germany and Canada, the only two jurisdictions where its Aurora Cannabis bid needed competition clearance, have both signed off.

Canada's Competition Bureau issued a no-action letter on 2 November and Germany's Federal Cartel Office cleared the deal on 3 November, after a German ministry approved the purchase of Aurora's German units on 20 October.
The offer of US$1 in cash plus 0.4013 Curaleaf shares per Aurora share still expires on 4 December, 19 days before Aurora holders vote on Organigram's rival C$7.80 deal.
On 9 November closing prices, the share part of Curaleaf's offer was worth about C$5.09 per Aurora share, while Aurora itself traded at C$7.30.
body: Curaleaf Holdings says the regulatory path for its hostile takeover of Aurora Cannabis is now clear. In a release on 10 November, the US operator said it had received every competition law clearance its offer needs, in Germany and in Canada, and argued that this makes its bid a surer and faster route to closing than the friendly deal Aurora's board has signed with Organigram Global.

The clearances remove one category of risk from Curaleaf's offer, but they do not change the basic arithmetic of the contest. Aurora's board backs Organigram's C$7.80-a-share agreement, Aurora's shareholders vote on it on 23 December, and Curaleaf's offer, unchanged since 6 October, expires on 4 December unless Curaleaf extends, amends or withdraws it. The next three weeks will show whether Curaleaf uses its regulatory head start to raise its price or lets the bid run out.

Curaleaf listed three separate approvals. On 20 October, Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy approved Curaleaf acquiring all the voting rights in three Aurora subsidiaries: Aurora Europe GmbH, Aurora Deutschland GmbH and Aurora Produktions GmbH. That is the foreign investment review that applies to buyers of German businesses. On 2 November, Canada's Competition Bureau sent a no-action letter saying its interim commissioner had finished her review and did not, at that time, intend to challenge the deal under section 92 of the Competition Act. On 3 November, Germany's Federal Cartel Office confirmed that the deal does not meet the conditions for a ban under German competition law and may go ahead.

Curaleaf said Germany and Canada were the only jurisdictions where competition clearance was required. Its release is careful on one point: the offer still depends on its other conditions being met or waived, so the clearances alone do not guarantee completion. Mugglehead, which reported the announcement, noted that it had not seen the regulators' letters themselves.

Chief executive Boris Jordan said in the release that the clearances leave a clear path for Aurora shareholders to take up the offer. Curaleaf went further in its pitch, saying Organigram's deal remains subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals and that Aurora investors should weigh that difference when comparing the two.
## Two offers, priced in different currencies

Curaleaf's amended offer pays US$1 in cash plus 0.4013 of a Curaleaf subordinate voting share for each Aurora share. Organigram's agreement, signed on 3 November, gives Aurora holders a choice of C$7.80 in cash, 5.8626 Organigram shares, or C$3.75 in cash plus 3.0431 Organigram shares, all subject to proration. The companies value that deal at about C$561 million on a fully diluted basis, as we reported on 6 November.

Market prices give a rough read on how investors see the contest. According to Mugglehead, Curaleaf closed at C$12.68 in Toronto on 9 November and Aurora at C$7.30. By MetaFlora's arithmetic, 0.4013 of a Curaleaf share at that price is worth about C$5.09. For Curaleaf's full offer to match Aurora's own trading price, the US$1 cash component would have to be worth about C$2.21, far more than a US dollar buys in Canadian currency. In other words, Aurora was trading well above the value of Curaleaf's bid and about C$0.50 below Organigram's C$7.80 cash price.
> A clean regulatory record is an advantage only if the price is competitive; on 9 November closing prices, the market was still paying more for Aurora than Curaleaf offers.

That gap matters because the value of Curaleaf's offer moves with Curaleaf's own share price, while Organigram's cash option is fixed. Organigram's share options are pegged to a reference price of about C$1.33, so their value also moves with Organigram's stock.

Organigram's route is longer. Its agreement is a court-supervised plan of arrangement in British Columbia, so it needs two-thirds of the votes cast by Aurora shareholders, a majority of the minority under Canadian rules, approval from Organigram's own shareholders for the new shares, a final court order and German foreign investment clearance. Aurora set the shareholder vote for 23 December, with a record date of 18 November, as we reported on 10 November. The companies target a January 2027 close.

Organigram's deal is anchored by British American Tobacco, which has agreed to buy about C$187.5 million of new Organigram shares at closing and has signed an irrevocable agreement to vote in favour. Aurora's board has rejected Curaleaf twice, first its original August terms and then the improved 6 October offer, arguing that the bid undervalued Aurora's EU-GMP plants and medical platforms.

The prize is international medical supply. Aurora sells medical cannabis in Canada, Europe, Australia and New Zealand and holds GMP-certified manufacturing in Canada and Germany. Organigram and Aurora say a combined company would run five facilities certified to EU good manufacturing practice standards and identify more than C$50 million in synergies. Curaleaf, according to its offer materials, projects at least US$40 million in potential savings across overhead, procurement and supply chains and pitches the deal as diversification across international markets, where its own revenue has been growing.

The German approvals Curaleaf now holds cover exactly the part of Aurora that both bidders value most: its German subsidiaries, which import, manufacture and distribute medical cannabis in Europe's largest medical market.

Three dates frame the contest. On 18 November, Aurora's register closes for the vote. On 4 December, Curaleaf's offer expires unless it is extended or changed, which is the point at which Curaleaf must decide whether to raise its terms, extend, or walk away. On 23 December, Aurora shareholders vote on Organigram's deal. Watch also for any move by Organigram to secure its own German clearance before the vote, and for the gap between Aurora's share price and the C$7.80 cash price, which is the market's running estimate of how likely the agreed deal is to close.
